analysis.one_liner: Gives working Americans a monthly tax credit and closes tax loopholes used by billionaires.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in the House and sent to the Ways and Means Committee, with no cosponsors and no action since.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would create a monthly tax credit paid to working Americans. It would also rewrite the tax code to close loopholes that let billionaires pay little or no federal income tax. It has just been introduced and is waiting in committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Working Americans would receive a monthly tax credit, spreading the money out over the year instead of a lump sum at tax time. Billionaires and very wealthy households, who currently use specialized tax strategies to pay low effective rates, would pay more if their loopholes were closed.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the tax code to provide a monthly credit to working Americans, delivering money each month rather than once a year at tax filing.
The bill also targets tax loopholes applicable to billionaires, requiring the wealthiest households to pay more of the taxes they now avoid.

analysis.who_pays: Very wealthy households, mainly billionaires, would bear the cost through higher tax payments once their loopholes are closed.

drawbacks.text: No bill text or summary beyond the title has been provided, so the size of the monthly credit, the income limits, and exactly which loopholes would be closed cannot be verified from the record.
The bill has no cosponsors, which suggests little early support in the House and raises the chance it never advances past committee.

Billionaire wealth is largely unrealized gains rather than yearly income, so a genuine billionaire tax would require major structural changes to the tax code that are technically and politically difficult to enact.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: If enacted as described, the bill would put a steady monthly payment into working households' pockets paid for by taxing the ultra-wealthy more heavily, a trade many would consider favorable. But the bill is one page of a title at this point: no text, no cost estimate, and no cosponsors, so there is no way yet to judge how generous the credit would be or how the loophole changes would actually work.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Ways and Means Committee, where it currently sits with no further action scheduled.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the House on September 14, 2026, by Rep. Greg Landsman.
On the same day it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the committee that handles tax legislation.
As of the latest record, the bill has zero cosponsors.
No further legislative action, hearing, or vote has been taken since the referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has won or lost anything: the bill sits in committee. Billionaires and ultra-wealthy households are better off by default because a bill that would raise their taxes has gained no cosponsors or momentum.

for.name: Rep. Greg Landsman
for.role: Sponsor, House Ways and Means Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and is its only sponsor so far.

sides.party_line_note: The only sponsor is a House Democrat and there are no cosponsors of either party yet, so the partisan shape is not established.

industries.note: The bill targets the loopholes this group uses to pay low effective tax rates, so they would pay significantly more if it passed. Their gain from the bill stalling is ordinary taxpayers' cost.

industries.industry: High-end tax planning and wealth management services
industries.note: Structures that let billionaires minimize taxes are this industry's product; closing the loopholes would shrink demand for them. Their interest runs against taxpayers who bear the shortfall.

analysis.trajectory: A first-term bill with no cosponsors referred to Ways and Means is very unlikely to get a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote in this Congress. It will most likely die in committee at the end of the session, as do the large majority of House tax bills without bipartisan sponsorship.
